subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Think about the last time the electricity in your home flickered on after dark. A single small bulb, or the glow of a phone screen, suddenly pushes back the night. In many homes across East Africa that light does not come from a distant power station at all — it comes from a solar panel on the roof charging a battery, which then powers lamps, a radio, and the charger for a mobile phone. Every one of those things works because of two invisible partners in nature that you will study in this unit: electricity and magnetism. They are so closely linked that scientists give them a single joined name, electromagnetism, and together they run almost every machine humans have ever built.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Describe a magnetic field, and understand that it surrounds a magnet and exerts a force on other magnetic fields.
Describe how to make an electromagnet and know that electromagnets have many applications.
Investigate factors that change the strength of an electromagnet.
Know that the reason the Earth has a magnetic field is that the core acts as a magnet.
Identify renewable resources (including wind, tidal and solar power, and bioplastics) and non-renewable resources (including fossil fuels), and describe how humans use them.
Use symbols and formulae to represent scientific ideas.
Decide what equipment is required to carry out an investigation or experiment and use it appropriately.

outcomes: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
Explain what an electric current is and describe how charge flows around a complete circuit.
Define and use the words current, voltage (potential difference) and resistance correctly, with their units.
Draw and recognise simple circuit diagrams using the correct symbols for a cell, battery, bulb, switch, ammeter and voltmeter.
Compare how current and voltage behave in series and parallel circuits.
Measure current with an ammeter and voltage with a voltmeter, connecting each the correct way.
Describe the relationship between current, voltage and resistance, and use it in simple calculations.
Explain what a magnet is, describe magnetic fields and poles, and state the rules of attraction and repulsion.
Explain how an electromagnet works and how to make it stronger, and give real uses of electromagnets.
Describe the motor effect and how an electric motor turns electrical energy into movement.

concepts.title: What Is Electric Current?
concepts.explanation:
Everything around you is made of tiny particles called atoms, and inside every atom are even smaller particles. Some of these carry a tiny amount of electric charge. In metals, some of these charged particles are free to move about, and when they all drift in the same direction along a wire, we have an electric current. So an electric current is simply the flow of electric charge. It is a little like water flowing through a pipe, except that instead of water it is charge that flows, and instead of a pipe it flows along a wire.

Current can only flow when there is a complete circuit — an unbroken loop of conductor leading from one end of a cell, through the wires and components, and back to the other end of the cell. If there is any gap in the loop, the current stops everywhere at once, just as water stops flowing if you cut the pipe. This is exactly why a switch works. A switch is nothing more than a controlled gap: when it is closed, the loop is complete and current flows; when it is open, there is a gap and the current stops. Turn off the switch on a solar lamp and the light dies instantly, because you have broken the loop.

Not every material lets current pass. A conductor is a material that current flows through easily, because it has charged particles that are free to move. Metals such as copper, aluminium and iron are excellent conductors, which is why wires are made of metal. An insulator is a material that current cannot flow through, because its charged particles are locked in place. Plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass and dry cloth are insulators. This difference is used everywhere for safety: the copper inside a wire carries the current, and the plastic coating around it stops the current escaping into your hand. Notice that the human body is a conductor — this is exactly why electricity is dangerous to touch.

By an old agreement that scientists still use, we draw conventional current as flowing from the positive end of the cell, round the circuit, and back to the negative end. You do not need to worry about the deep details yet; what matters is that the current flows in a loop, always in the same direction, driven by the cell. Every cell has a positive end (marked +) and a negative end (marked -), and connecting them the correct way round is part of making a circuit work.
concepts.example: Did You Know? A current of just one ampere means an enormous number of charged particles — roughly six billion billion of them — passing a point every single second. Copper is used for almost all wiring because it conducts electricity extremely well and can be pulled into thin, bendy wires without breaking.

concepts.title: Voltage, the Push Behind the Current
concepts.explanation:
If current is the flow of charge, something must push that charge around the loop. That push is called voltage, and it comes from the cell or battery. The proper scientific name for voltage is potential difference, but in everyday use we simply say voltage. Voltage is measured in volts (V).

Think of the cell as a pump and the current as water flowing round a loop of pipe. The pump does not create the water — it pushes it round. In the same way, the cell does not create charge — it provides the energy that pushes the charge around the circuit. The bigger the voltage, the stronger the push, and (for the same components) the bigger the current that flows. A single dry cell of the kind used in a torch gives about 1.5 V. When you stack cells together to make a battery, their voltages add up: two 1.5 V cells in a line give 3 V, and four give 6 V. That is why a torch that needs more power holds several cells stacked end to end.

A cell is only a store, though, and the energy inside it had to come from somewhere — so did the electricity in a wall socket. Some of the resources we draw that energy from are renewable, which means nature replaces them about as fast as we use them: sunlight caught by a solar panel, wind turning a turbine, and the rise and fall of the tide. Plants count as renewable too, which is why bioplastics can be made from them instead of from oil. Other resources are non-renewable. Coal, oil and natural gas took many millions of years to form underground, and once they are burned they are gone for good. The difference matters to a whole country, not just to a science lesson: building on renewable resources means the lights still come on long after the coal would have run out.
concepts.example: Inside a cell, stored chemical energy is turned into electrical energy that pushes the current. This is why batteries eventually go flat — the chemicals are used up, the voltage falls, and the push gets weaker until the bulb dims and dies. A solar panel does the same job in a different way: instead of chemicals, it uses the energy of sunlight to provide the voltage that pushes the current. During the day the panel pushes current to charge a battery; at night the battery takes over and pushes the current itself. Understanding voltage as a push, and the cell or panel as the source of energy, is one of the most important ideas in this whole unit.

concepts.title: Resistance, Slowing the Current Down
concepts.explanation:
The third big idea is resistance. Resistance is how much a component slows down the current that tries to pass through it. Everything in a circuit has some resistance, even the wires, but some components resist much more than others. Resistance is measured in ohms.

As the charged particles drift along, they keep bumping into the fixed particles of the material and are slowed down. A material or component that makes this harder has a high resistance; one that lets charge slip through easily has a low resistance. Several things change how much resistance a wire has:

A longer wire has more resistance than a short one, because the charge has further to travel and more particles to bump into.

A thinner wire has more resistance than a thick one, because there is less room for the charge to move through.

Some materials naturally resist more than others. Copper resists very little, which is why we use it for wires; the special thin wire inside a bulb resists a lot, which is why it heats up and glows.

These three ideas are joined by one simple rule. For a fixed voltage, more resistance means less current, and less resistance means more current. Picture squeezing a pipe: pinch it (more resistance) and less water flows; open it wide (less resistance) and more water flows. In the same way, if you add more resistance to a circuit while the battery stays the same, the current drops. And if you raise the voltage while the resistance stays the same, the current rises. Scientists write this relationship as a neat word equation:

This means that if you know any two of the three quantities, you can work out the third. You can rearrange it to find current (current = voltage / resistance) or to find resistance (resistance = voltage / current). You will practise using this rule in the Worked Examples below — it is one of the most useful relationships in all of physics.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The thin wire inside an old-style light bulb, called a filament, has such high resistance that the current heats it until it glows white-hot and gives off light. A toaster and an electric heater use the very same trick: current is pushed through a high-resistance wire until it gets hot enough to toast bread or warm a room.

concepts.title: Circuits: Series and Parallel
concepts.explanation:
Now that you know about current, voltage and resistance, you can understand how components are joined together. There are two main ways to build a circuit, and they behave very differently. Learning to tell them apart is a key skill of this unit.

Scientists do not draw pictures of real bulbs and batteries every time — it would take too long and look untidy. Instead they use a set of agreed symbols to draw a neat circuit diagram. You should learn these common symbols:

A cell is drawn as one long thin line and one short thick line side by side (the long line is the positive end).

A battery is two or more cells drawn in a row.

A bulb (lamp) is drawn as a circle with a cross inside it.

A switch is drawn as a small gap with a line that can close it like a lever.

An ammeter is a circle with a letter A inside it; a voltmeter is a circle with a letter V inside it.

Wires are drawn as straight lines joining everything into a loop.

A series circuit has just one loop. All the components are joined end to end, one after another, so the current has only one path to follow. This gives series circuits two important behaviours that you must remember:

The current is the same everywhere in a series circuit. Because there is only one path, the same current flows through every component — the cell, each bulb and the wires.

The voltage is shared between the components. If a 3 V battery drives two identical bulbs in series, each bulb gets about 1.5 V. The bulbs are dimmer than a single bulb would be on its own.

A series circuit has a big weakness. Because it is a single loop, if one component breaks, the whole circuit breaks. Take out one bulb, or let one bulb burn out, and every bulb goes dark, because the loop now has a gap. Old strings of decorative lights worked this way, which is why one dead bulb could switch off the whole string.

A parallel circuit gives the current more than one path by splitting it into separate branches. Each bulb sits on its own branch, like separate side-roads leaving and rejoining a main road. Parallel circuits behave in the opposite way to series circuits in two important ways:

Each branch gets the full voltage. If a 3 V battery drives two bulbs in parallel, each bulb gets the full 3 V, so the bulbs are bright, as bright as a single bulb on its own.

Each branch can work on its own. If one bulb breaks, the others stay lit, because each has its own complete loop back to the battery. The current simply keeps flowing through the branches that are still whole.

This is exactly why the lights and sockets in a house are wired in parallel. If your home were wired in series, switching off one lamp would plunge every room into darkness, and a single blown bulb would kill all the power. Because the house is wired in parallel, each light and socket has its own branch: you can switch one on or off, and a fault in one does not stop the rest. The same is true of a solar-powered home — each lamp and each phone charger is on its own branch so one can fail without darkening the others.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Every room in a house shares the same voltage from the mains because the rooms are wired in parallel — that is why a lamp is just as bright whether it is the only thing switched on or one of many. In a series circuit, adding more bulbs makes them all dimmer, because the same voltage has to be shared among more of them.

concepts.title: Measuring Current and Voltage
concepts.explanation:
A real scientist does not just guess how much current flows — they measure it. There are two instruments you must know, and each is connected in its own special way.

An ammeter measures the current in amps. Because the current has to pass through it to be counted, an ammeter is always connected in series — it becomes part of the single loop, so that all the current flows through it, like a gate that counts everything passing along the road. If you break the loop and slot the ammeter into the gap, it will read the current flowing at that point.

A voltmeter measures the voltage across a component in volts. Voltage is a difference in push between two points, so a voltmeter is connected in parallel — across the component, touching the wire on each side of it, like measuring the height of a step by standing beside it rather than walking through it. Connect a voltmeter across a bulb and it tells you how many volts are being used up pushing current through that bulb.
concepts.example: A simple way to remember the difference: the Ammeter goes Along the circuit (in series), while the Voltmeter goes aVer, or across, the component (in parallel). Getting these connections right is a real practical skill, and using them lets you check the rules you learned in Part 4 — for example, that current is the same everywhere in a series circuit, and that each branch of a parallel circuit gets the full voltage.

concepts.title: Magnets and Magnetic Fields
concepts.explanation:
We now turn to the second half of the unit: magnetism. At first it may seem completely separate from electricity, but you will soon see that the two are deeply connected. Let us start with what a magnet is.

A magnet is an object that can attract certain metals and that always has two poles, called the north pole and the south pole. The force of a magnet is strongest at its poles. There is one golden rule of magnets that you must know by heart:

This means two north poles push each other away, and two south poles push each other away, but a north pole and a south pole pull together. You can feel this yourself with two fridge magnets: turn them one way and they snap together, turn one around and they push apart so strongly you can hardly force them to meet.

Only a few materials are magnetic — that is, attracted to a magnet. The main ones are iron, steel (which is mostly iron), nickel and cobalt. Most other materials, including copper, aluminium, plastic, wood and glass, are not magnetic and are not pulled by a magnet at all. This is why a magnet will pick up an iron nail or a steel spoon but ignore a copper coin or a plastic ruler. Note the difference from electricity here: copper is a brilliant electrical conductor but is not magnetic, while iron is magnetic — so 'metal' does not automatically mean 'magnetic'.

Around every magnet there is an invisible region where its force can be felt, called the magnetic field. We cannot see it, but we can map its shape. If you scatter tiny iron filings on a sheet of paper over a bar magnet, they line up in curved lines running from the north pole to the south pole, showing the shape of the field. These lines are called field lines. They are closest together near the poles, where the field is strongest, and spread further apart away from the magnet, where the field is weaker. A compass is simply a tiny magnet that is free to turn, and it lines itself up with whatever magnetic field it is in.

Here is one of the most wonderful facts in science: the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, with a magnetic field stretching all around it. The reason lies deep inside the planet. The Earth's core is mostly iron, and its outer part is liquid and always moving. That moving iron acts like a magnet, and it is what gives the whole Earth its magnetic field. This is why a compass works. The compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with the Earth's field, so one end always swings round to point roughly north. Travellers have used this for hundreds of years to find their way across deserts and oceans. For a Muslim family far from home, a compass helps find the qibla — the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah — so they can face the right way for prayer. A simple magnet, and the invisible field of the whole planet, guides them.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The Earth's magnetic field also protects all life on the planet by turning away much of the harmful particles that stream out from the Sun. The needle of a compass does not point to the exact geographic North Pole, but to a slightly different magnetic pole — sailors and pilots have to allow for this small difference.

methods.title: Building Your First Circuit (Battery, Wire and Bulb)
methods.example: To build a complete circuit that lights a bulb, and to prove that current only flows when the loop is complete.
steps: Tape one wire to the flat negative (-) end of the battery, and touch its other end to the metal base of the bulb.
Tape a second wire to the bump on the positive (+) end of the battery, and touch its other end to the side of the bulb, so the bulb sits in a complete loop.
Observe: does the bulb light? You have made a complete circuit.
Now lift one wire away from the bulb to make a gap in the loop. Watch what happens to the bulb.
Reconnect it, then add a second battery in a line (positive of one to negative of the next) and watch the brightness.

methods.title: Series versus Parallel Bulbs
methods.example: To compare how bulbs behave when wired in series (one loop) and in parallel (separate branches).
steps: SERIES: Connect the two bulbs one after the other in a single loop with the battery, so the current must pass through both. Note how bright they are.
While the series circuit is lit, remove one bulb (or lift its wire). Watch what happens to the other bulb.
PARALLEL: Now re-wire so each bulb has its own loop back to the battery (two branches side by side). Note how bright they are compared with the series bulbs.
While the parallel circuit is lit, remove one bulb. Watch what happens to the other bulb.
Record everything in the table below.

methods.title: Make an Electromagnet (Battery, Nail and Wire)
methods.example: To build a working electromagnet and to find out what makes it stronger.
steps: Wind the wire neatly around the nail about 20 times, all in the same direction, leaving a length of wire free at each end.
Tape one bared end of the wire to the + end of the battery and the other bared end to the — end, so current flows through the coil. (Do this just before testing, and disconnect between tests.)
Bring the tip of the nail close to the pile of paperclips and count how many it picks up.
Disconnect the battery. Watch what happens to the paperclips — do they fall off?
Now wind about 20 MORE turns of wire onto the nail (about 40 in total), reconnect, and count the paperclips again.

methods.title: Magnetic or Not? Poles and Field Mapping
methods.example: To find out which materials are magnetic, to test the rule of poles, and to map a magnetic field with a compass.
steps: Touch the magnet to each object in turn. Sort them into two groups: attracted (magnetic) and not attracted.
If you have two magnets, bring two ends together, then turn one around and bring them together again. Feel the attraction and the repulsion.
Place a bar magnet on the paper and set the compass at several points around it. At each point, draw a small arrow showing the way the compass needle points.
Join up your arrows to draw the curved field lines running from one pole to the other.
Record which objects were magnetic and what you felt with the two magnets.

workedExamples.title: Current, Voltage and Resistance
workedExamples.prompt: Follow the reasoning in each example. In every one, notice how we use the rule voltage = current x resistance and the behaviour of series and parallel circuits.
workedExamples.solution:
Worked Example 1 — Finding the current

Question: Khadija connects a bulb of resistance 3 ohms to a battery giving 6 V. What current flows through the bulb?

Step 1 — Choose the right form of the rule. We want the current, so use current = voltage / resistance.

Step 2 — Put in the numbers. current = 6 V / 3 ohms = 2. So the current is 2 A.

workedExamples.title: 1 - Finding the current
workedExamples.prompt: Question: Khadija connects a bulb of resistance 3 ohms to a battery giving 6 V. What current flows through the bulb?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Choose the right form of the rule. We want the current, so use current = voltage / resistance.

Step 2 — Put in the numbers. current = 6 V / 3 ohms = 2. So the current is 2 A.

Answer: A current of 2 amps flows through the bulb. Notice that if the resistance were larger, the same 6 V would push a smaller current.

Worked Example 2 — Finding the voltage

workedExamples.title: 2 - Finding the voltage
workedExamples.prompt: Question: A current of 0.5 A flows through a component with a resistance of 4 ohms. What is the voltage across it?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Choose the right form of the rule. We want the voltage, so use voltage = current x resistance.

Step 2 — Put in the numbers. voltage = 0.5 A x 4 ohms = 2. So the voltage is 2 V.

Answer: The voltage across the component is 2 V. This is the push being used up driving the current through that component.

Worked Example 3 — Series circuit voltage sharing

workedExamples.title: 3 - Series circuit voltage sharing
workedExamples.prompt: Question: Yusuf connects two identical bulbs in series to a 3 V battery. Roughly what voltage does each bulb get, and how does the current in the two bulbs compare?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Voltage. In a series circuit the voltage is shared between the components. Two identical bulbs share the 3 V equally, so each gets about 1.5 V.

Step 2 — Current. In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere, so exactly the same current flows through both bulbs.

Answer: Each bulb gets about 1.5 V, and the same current flows through both. Because each bulb has only half the battery's voltage, the two bulbs are dimmer than a single bulb would be.

Worked Example 4 — Parallel circuit voltage

workedExamples.title: 4 - Parallel circuit voltage
workedExamples.prompt: Question: Halima now connects the same two bulbs in parallel across the 3 V battery. What voltage does each bulb get, and what happens if one bulb breaks?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Voltage. In a parallel circuit each branch gets the full battery voltage, so each bulb gets the whole 3 V and shines brightly.

Step 2 — One bulb breaks. Each bulb has its own complete loop, so if one breaks, the other keeps its full voltage and stays lit.

Answer: Each bulb gets the full 3 V and is bright, and if one bulb breaks the other still works. This is why homes are wired in parallel.

Reading Comprehension — Light After Sunset in Garissa

activities.title: Building Your First Circuit (Battery, Wire and Bulb)
activities.materials: One or two 1.5 V batteries (torch cells).; A small torch bulb (or a small LED, with an adult's help).; Two or three pieces of insulated wire with the ends bared (an adult strips the plastic).; Sticky tape to hold the wire ends to the battery.
steps: Tape one wire to the flat negative (-) end of the battery, and touch its other end to the metal base of the bulb.
Tape a second wire to the bump on the positive (+) end of the battery, and touch its other end to the side of the bulb, so the bulb sits in a complete loop.
Observe: does the bulb light? You have made a complete circuit.
Now lift one wire away from the bulb to make a gap in the loop. Watch what happens to the bulb.
Reconnect it, then add a second battery in a line (positive of one to negative of the next) and watch the brightness.
Safety: Use only a small 1.5 V battery. Never use plug sockets or mains electricity, and disconnect the battery when you finish.

activities.title: Series versus Parallel Bulbs
activities.materials: One or two 1.5 V batteries.; Two identical small bulbs (in holders if you have them, or held with tape).; Several pieces of wire with bared ends.; Sticky tape.
steps: SERIES: Connect the two bulbs one after the other in a single loop with the battery, so the current must pass through both. Note how bright they are.
While the series circuit is lit, remove one bulb (or lift its wire). Watch what happens to the other bulb.
PARALLEL: Now re-wire so each bulb has its own loop back to the battery (two branches side by side). Note how bright they are compared with the series bulbs.
While the parallel circuit is lit, remove one bulb. Watch what happens to the other bulb.
Record everything in the table below.
Safety: Use only a small 1.5 V battery. Never use plug sockets or mains electricity, and disconnect the battery when you finish.

activities.title: Make an Electromagnet (Battery, Nail and Wire)
activities.materials: A large iron nail (steel nails work well too).; About one metre of thin insulated wire with the ends bared.; One or two 1.5 V batteries.; A small pile of steel paperclips or pins to pick up.; Sticky tape.
steps: Wind the wire neatly around the nail about 20 times, all in the same direction, leaving a length of wire free at each end.
Tape one bared end of the wire to the + end of the battery and the other bared end to the — end, so current flows through the coil. (Do this just before testing, and disconnect between tests.)
Bring the tip of the nail close to the pile of paperclips and count how many it picks up.
Disconnect the battery. Watch what happens to the paperclips — do they fall off?
Now wind about 20 MORE turns of wire onto the nail (about 40 in total), reconnect, and count the paperclips again.

Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards. Use only a small 1.5 V battery. Never use plug sockets or mains electricity, and disconnect the battery when you finish.

activities.title: Magnetic or Not? Poles and Field Mapping
activities.materials: One or two magnets (fridge magnets or bar magnets).; A small compass (or use a magnetised needle floated on water).; A collection of small objects: iron nail, steel spoon, copper coin, aluminium foil, plastic ruler, wooden peg, glass marble.; A sheet of paper and a pencil.
steps: Touch the magnet to each object in turn. Sort them into two groups: attracted (magnetic) and not attracted.
If you have two magnets, bring two ends together, then turn one around and bring them together again. Feel the attraction and the repulsion.
Place a bar magnet on the paper and set the compass at several points around it. At each point, draw a small arrow showing the way the compass needle points.
Join up your arrows to draw the curved field lines running from one pole to the other.
Record which objects were magnetic and what you felt with the two magnets.

Safety: Magnets must never go in or near your mouth — swallowing magnets is a medical emergency. Keep them away from babies and young children. Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: Observe: Measuring Current and Voltage
activities.materials: One or two 1.5 V batteries (torch cells).; A small torch bulb (or a small LED, with an adult's help).; Two or three pieces of insulated wire with the ends bared (an adult strips the plastic).; Sticky tape to hold the wire ends to the battery.
steps: Look for an example of measuring current and voltage around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Electric current and Voltage (potential difference).
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Ammeters in Series, Voltmeters Across
rules.text: An ammeter measures CURRENT and is connected IN SERIES (in the loop). A voltmeter measures VOLTAGE and is connected IN PARALLEL (across a component). Ammeter = Along; Voltmeter = across (aVer).

rules.title: Electrical Safety Rules
rules.text: Experiments use ONLY 1.5 V batteries — NEVER mains electricity. Never touch anything electrical with wet hands. Never short a battery by joining its ends with just a wire. In a thunderstorm, go indoors and stay away from tall lone objects and water.

rules.title: A Way to Remember the Meters
rules.text: Remember the meters. Ammeter = Along (series); Voltmeter = across (parallel). Repeat it until it sticks.

rules.title: Current, Voltage and Resistance
rules.text: Current is the flow of charge; voltage is the push that drives it; resistance slows it down. Voltage = current x resistance. Series: one loop, same current everywhere, shared voltage. Parallel: separate branches, full voltage on each, one can fail without stopping the rest. Electricity makes magnetism (electromagnets); magnetism plus current makes movement (the motor effect). Stay safe: 1.5 V batteries only, never the mains, never with wet hands.

terms: Electric current
The flow of electric charge around a circuit; measured in amperes (A).
Voltage (potential difference)
The push from a cell that drives the current; measured in volts (V).
Resistance
How much a component slows the current; measured in ohms.
Cell
A single source of voltage using stored chemical energy (about 1.5 V).
Battery
Two or more cells joined together; their voltages add up.
Circuit
A complete loop of conductors that lets current flow.
Conductor
A material that lets current pass easily (copper, metal, the body).
Insulator
A material that does not let current pass (plastic, rubber, glass).
Series circuit
One single loop; same current everywhere, shared voltage.
Parallel circuit
Separate branches; each branch gets the full voltage.
Ammeter
Measures current in amps; connected in series.
Voltmeter
Measures voltage in volts; connected in parallel (across a component).

realProblems.answer: 1. During the day, the solar panel uses sunlight to provide voltage that pushes current to light the lamps and to charge the battery. During the night, the battery gives back its stored energy and pushes the current itself, so the lamps still work after dark.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what an electric current is and why a circuit must be a complete loop.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1. An electric current is the flow of electric charge around a circuit. The circuit must be a complete loop because charge can only flow if there is an unbroken path from one end of the cell, through the components, and back to the other end; any gap stops the current everywhere.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between voltage and current using the water-in-a-pipe picture.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 2. Voltage is the push, like a pump driving water round a loop of pipe. Current is the flow, like the water actually moving. The cell provides the voltage that pushes the current (the charge) round the circuit.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is resistance? Name two things that increase the resistance of a wire.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 3. Resistance is how much a component slows down the current. Resistance is increased by making a wire longer and by making it thinner (and some materials resist more than others).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: State the rule that links voltage, current and resistance.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 4. Voltage = current x resistance. For a fixed voltage, more resistance means less current; more voltage (same resistance) means more current.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe how current and voltage behave in a series circuit.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 5. In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere (one path), and the voltage is shared between the components, so bulbs are dimmer than one bulb alone.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe how current and voltage behave in a parallel circuit.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 6. In a parallel circuit each branch gets the full voltage, so bulbs are bright, and each branch has its own loop, so one branch can fail without stopping the others.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit you will be able to:
I can explain what an electric current is and describe how charge flows around a complete circuit.
I can define and use the words current, voltage (potential difference) and resistance correctly, with their units.
I can draw and recognise simple circuit diagrams using the correct symbols for a cell, battery, bulb, switch, ammeter and voltmeter.
I can compare how current and voltage behave in series and parallel circuits.
I can measure current with an ammeter and voltage with a voltmeter, connecting each the correct way.
I can describe the relationship between current, voltage and resistance, and use it in simple calculations.
I can explain what a magnet is, describe magnetic fields and poles, and state the rules of attraction and repulsion.
